title: The Tibetan Book of the Dead, or The After-Death Experiences on the Bardo Plane (Bardo Thödol)
author: attributed to Padmasambhava, revealed by Karma Lingpa (14th c.); ed. W. Y. Evans-Wentz
edition_cited: First edition, London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1927
locator_hints: Book I, Part I: 'The Bardo of the Moments of Death', instructions on the Primary and Secondary Clear Light (search 'setting-face-to-face with the Clear Light')
Book I, Part II: the Chönyid Bardo, days one to seven: bright lights of the five wisdoms paired with dull lights, and the instruction not to flee the bright one
search 'who have meditated upon the Great Perfection' for the remark on prior training
Evans-Wentz's footnotes on the death-process signs and on yogic rehearsal
summary: The classic guide read to the dying and dead, in its first English edition. It is not a sitting-practice manual, but it is the tradition's instruction on what to do when light appears: the Clear Light at the moment of death is to be recognised as one's own mind and rested in; in the following days dazzling coloured radiances appear together with dull, comfortable lights, and the hearer is told to trust the dazzling light and not be drawn to the dull one; sounds, rays and forms are to be known as one's own projections. The text says that those trained in life by a teacher's 'setting-face-to-face' recognise at once, and mentions meditators of the Great Perfection and Great Symbol. Evans-Wentz's notes add yogic glosses.
why_relevant: Public-domain primary instruction on recognising and responding to light phenomena, framed as post-death but explicitly tied to prior meditative training; marginal for this library because no living practice method for producing light is given.

date_evidence.basis: title page of the scanned edition: 'London: Humphrey Milford, 1927'; preface dated 'Easter, 1927'

found_via: own lead: public-domain Tibetan translations on archive.org
notes: Likely to be judged marginal or dropped: the lights described are after-death experiences, and the BRIEF excludes near-death light without a practice account. Kept as a candidate because the text is instruction on how to meet arising light and names prior training as the condition for recognition. OCR is rough. Evans-Wentz's editorial notes mix in Theosophical and Hindu-yoga comparisons.
